skip_reason: Rescheduling call on an existing booked job, not new business. Shelley Kasiske already has a crew confirmed for the next morning to unload a pod ('you guys are supposed to come tomorrow morning to my house to help unload a pod') and is calling because the pod will not fit in her driveway. The entire call is logistics and re-dating on that booked move — canceling tomorrow, checking Tuesday availability, and adding a pickup leg from the pod facility. Some pricing surfaces ('$960'), but it is a revised figure on work already sold, with no quote form, intake, differentiator pitch or booking of a new move, so per the skip rule this is an existing-job call with a little pricing in it. The 85-point sales scorecard does not apply.
top_strength: Rance solved a genuinely messy logistics problem quickly and gave the customer real numbers rather than a callback promise. He checked live availability, was straight about the constraint ('Monday, we're actually pretty booked out'), and priced the new plan on the spot with the assumption stated out loud and deliberately padded: 'just cause we're going to be loading it from the pods into the truck and then to drive, I would say to add two hours on which probably is kind of conservative... we at around $960.' He also protected her from a no-show charge by clearing the dead booking himself — 'I'm gonna go ahead and take it off the books for tomorrow since we know we can't do it tomorrow' — and problem-solved alongside her on the street-permit angle rather than just declining, which prompted her own 'maybe the street maybe that's my other option too.' She closed with 'Okay, perfect. Okay, thank you.'
coaching_note: The call ended with the next step owned by the customer instead of by Einstein: 'if you want to give me a callback on Monday with the address of where the pods going to be and stuff like that, we can kind of get it all set up for you on Tuesday.' She has two pods, no confirmed pickup address, no held Tuesday slot and a canceled Saturday — that is a lot of open loops riding on her remembering to call. Better: hold the Tuesday morning window under her name now, tell her it is held, and commit to calling her Monday rather than waiting. Same for the price — $960 was quoted verbally and nothing was sent to confirm it, so the one thing she can point back to on Tuesday is her own memory of the number. A short confirmation email with the held time and the estimate, and an ask to reply if anything is wrong, closes both gaps in about two minutes.
phone_presence_notes: Friendly and genuinely collaborative — he validated her constraint ('Oh, okay, I gotcha. That makes sense') and offered options rather than a flat no — but the warmth is task-shaped rather than personal, her name is never used, and several answers come out in fragments ('Eight foot and. 63 hours drive down. How I would say four hours.') that force her to re-ask.
audio_review_reason: Transcript quality is poor enough to limit the read: Rance's side contains multiple garbled or truncated fragments ('63 hours drive down', 'Should I do it. Hang, I'm sorry', 'It's just now really rate that includes the truck fee') and both speakers' lines are interleaved out of sequence, so it is unclear whether he was actually disjointed or the transcription dropped words. Audio would also confirm the $960 estimate and the Tuesday availability were communicated as clearly as the summary reads, since the customer is leaving with no written record of either.
